articles.title: Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months
articles.summary: A new clinical trial found that the ketogenic diet dramatically outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in reducing liver fat and improving metabolic health, even when participants lost similar amounts of weight. After just four to five months, about half of those following keto no longer met the criteria for prediabetes, while their liver fat dropped by an average of 67%.
articles.content:
A ketogenic diet may offer significant health benefits beyond weight loss, according to a new clinical trial that compared three popular approaches to eating. Researchers found that people following a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet experienced substantially greater reductions in liver fat than those eating Mediterranean or low-fat diets, even though all three groups lost similar amounts of weight.

The results were especially striking for people with prediabetes. After just four to five months on a ketogenic (or "Keto") diet, approximately half of the participants no longer met the diagnostic criteria for the condition. The findings, published in the journal Cell Metabolism, suggest that the types of foods people eat can influence metabolic health in ways that extend beyond the number of pounds they lose.

"We know weight loss can improve metabolic health in people who are obese," says Samuel Klein, the study's corresponding author at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Missouri. "Our data suggest that if you have high liver fat content and prediabetes, reducing carbohydrate intake can have important therapeutic effects on metabolism beyond just weight loss alone."

Comparing Keto, Mediterranean, and Low-Fat Diets

An estimated 40% of American adults have obesity, a condition associated with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease, and other health problems. Doctors frequently recommend dietary changes to help patients lose weight and improve their metabolic health, which refers to how effectively the body manages energy, blood sugar, and fats.

Three commonly recommended approaches are low-carbohydrate diets, low-fat diets, and Mediterranean diets. Although each can support weight loss, researchers have been uncertain whether one offers additional metabolic advantages when the amount of weight lost is roughly the same.

These eating patterns differ substantially in their nutritional makeup. Low-carbohydrate approaches, including Atkins and ketogenic diets, restrict carbohydrate consumption, while low-fat diets may obtain as much as 70% of their calories from carbohydrates. The Mediterranean diet emphasizes plant foods such as vegetables, nuts, and olive oil, along with moderate amounts of fish and dairy. Ketogenic diets, meanwhile, can include considerable amounts of fat from animal products, including saturated fat.

To compare their effects, Klein and his colleagues recruited 42 adults with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. Prediabetes occurs when blood sugar levels rise above the normal range but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Fatty liver disease involves excess fat accumulating inside liver cells, which can interfere with the body's ability to regulate metabolism.

A Controlled Clinical Trial With Similar Weight Loss

Participants were randomly assigned to follow one of three diets: ketogenic, Mediterranean, or a low-fat diet emphasizing plant-based foods. To ensure that participants followed their assigned eating plans, the research team supplied all their meals and arranged weekly consultations with a dietitian.

The diets had sharply different proportions of carbohydrates and fat. In the ketogenic group, carbohydrates accounted for just 4% of daily calories, while fat supplied 73%. The Mediterranean group received 50% of its calories from carbohydrates and 35% from fat. The plant-forward group consumed 70% of its calories from carbohydrates and 15% from fat.

Researchers adjusted calorie intake individually so that participants across all three groups lost approximately 10% of their starting body weight. Reaching this target took about four to five months.

By the end of the intervention, every group had experienced meaningful reductions in body fat and improvements in insulin sensitivity. Insulin is the hormone that helps move sugar from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy. Greater insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

However, the similarities between the groups largely ended there.

Keto Diet Reduces Liver Fat by 67%

The ketogenic diet produced the largest improvements in several important indicators of liver function and metabolic health.

Participants following keto experienced an average 67% reduction in liver fat, compared with a 45% reduction in both the Mediterranean and low-fat groups. Because the groups lost comparable amounts of weight, the difference suggests that carbohydrate restriction may influence liver fat through mechanisms beyond weight loss alone.

To investigate these effects, the researchers collected blood samples repeatedly over a 24-hour period, allowing them to observe changes in hormones involved in energy metabolism.

The ketogenic group showed the greatest increase in glucagon, a hormone that helps regulate the body's energy supply and promotes the reduction of fat stored in the liver. Participants on keto also experienced the largest decrease in insulin levels, another change that can help reduce liver fat accumulation.

One result was particularly unexpected. Despite getting nearly three-quarters of their calories from fat, the keto participants did not show an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels during the study.

"The most surprising finding was that participants in the ketogenic diet group didn't experience an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels despite consuming the most fat," says Max Petersen, the study's first author at Washington University School of Medicine.

Half of Keto Participants No Longer Had Prediabetes

The benefits extended beyond liver fat. After the weight-loss intervention, approximately 50% of participants assigned to the ketogenic diet no longer met the criteria for prediabetes. By comparison, that milestone was reached by 29% of those on the Mediterranean diet and just 7% of those following the low-fat, plant-forward diet.

These differences are notable because prediabetes signals an elevated risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Bringing blood sugar levels below the prediabetes threshold is an important improvement, although it does not necessarily mean the condition has been permanently reversed.

The findings also highlight a potentially important distinction in weight management: losing weight and improving metabolic health are closely connected, but they are not necessarily the same thing. The composition of a diet may affect how the body handles blood sugar, stores fat, and responds to hormones, even when weight loss is similar.

Researchers emphasize the growing importance of understanding these effects as powerful new obesity treatments become more widely available. GLP-1 medications, which act on hormone pathways involved in appetite and blood sugar regulation, have transformed the treatment of obesity by helping many patients achieve substantial weight loss.

"GLP-1-based medications have revolutionized the therapy of obesity. We now have a very effective pharmacotherapy for achieving significant weight loss," Petersen says. "But in addition, our study shows that the specific composition of the diet can give you added benefits."

Although the trial was relatively small and lasted only four to five months, its carefully controlled design offers evidence that dietary composition can play an important role in metabolic health. Longer studies involving more participants will be needed to determine whether the benefits persist and how different diets compare over time.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health and the Foundation for Barnes-Jewish Hospital.

This has broad implications for millions with obesity, fatty liver disease, and prediabetes, offering a promising dietary approach to improve health outcomes. The study is detailed, focused, and presents a meaningful advancement in nutritional therapy for metabolic diseases.
articles.personality_title: Keto diet cuts liver fat by two-thirds and helps reverse prediabetes in 4 months
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many adults with obesity also have extra fat in their livers and higher blood sugar levels, which can lead to serious health problems like type 2 diabetes. Doctors often suggest diets like Mediterranean, low-fat, or low-carb to help improve health and lose weight. But it wasn’t clear which diet helps the liver and blood sugar the most.

**What happened** – A clinical trial tested three diets—ketogenic (very low-carb, high-fat), Mediterranean, and low-fat—in 42 adults with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. Each person lost about 10% of their body weight over 4 to 5 months. The researchers gave all meals and checked participants’ health regularly. The keto group ate only 4% of calories from carbs and 73% from fat, while the other groups ate more carbs and less fat.

**Impact** – The keto diet lowered liver fat by 67%, much more than the 45% drop seen with the other diets. About half of the keto group no longer had prediabetes after the study, compared to fewer in the other groups. This shows that eating fewer carbs and more fat can improve liver health and blood sugar in ways that weight loss alone does not explain. Surprisingly, the keto group did not have increased blood fat or cholesterol despite eating the most fat.

**What's next step** – Researchers want to run bigger and longer studies to see if these health benefits last and how different diets compare over time. They also hope to combine diet changes with new medicines that help with weight loss and blood sugar control to better treat obesity and related conditions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A ketogenic diet greatly reduces liver fat and improves blood sugar control beyond weight loss, offering a powerful option for people with obesity and prediabetes.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le régime keto réduit la graisse du foie de deux tiers et aide à inverser le prédiabète en 4 mois
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – De nombreux adultes en surpoids ont également un excès de graisse dans le foie et un taux de sucre élevé dans le sang, ce qui peut entraîner des problèmes graves comme le diabète de type 2. Les médecins recommandent souvent des régimes méditerranéen, pauvre en graisses ou pauvre en glucides pour améliorer la santé et perdre du poids. Mais on ne savait pas quel régime était le plus efficace pour le foie et le sucre sanguin.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Un essai clinique a testé trois régimes—keto (très pauvre en glucides, riche en graisses), méditerranéen et pauvre en graisses—chez 42 adultes avec obésité, prédiabète et stéatose hépatique. Chaque participant a perdu environ 10 % de son poids en 4 à 5 mois. Les chercheurs ont fourni tous les repas et suivi la santé des participants régulièrement. Le groupe keto consommait seulement 4 % de calories en glucides et 73 % en graisses, tandis que les autres groupes mangeaient plus de glucides et moins de graisses.

**Impact** – Le régime keto a réduit la graisse du foie de 67 %, beaucoup plus que les 45 % observés avec les autres régimes. Environ la moitié du groupe keto n’était plus en situation de prédiabète à la fin de l’étude, contre moins dans les autres groupes. Cela montre que manger moins de glucides et plus de graisses peut améliorer la santé du foie et le contrôle du sucre dans le sang, au-delà de la perte de poids seule. Fait surprenant, le groupe keto n’a pas vu augmenter ses taux de graisses ou de cholestérol dans le sang, malgré la forte consommation de graisses.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs souhaitent réaliser des études plus larges et plus longues pour vérifier si ces bénéfices durent et comparer les différents régimes sur le long terme. Ils veulent aussi combiner ces changements alimentaires avec de nouveaux médicaments qui aident à perdre du poids et à contrôler le sucre sanguin pour mieux traiter l’obésité et ses complications.

**En une phrase** – Un régime cétogène réduit fortement la graisse du foie et améliore le contrôle du sucre sanguin au-delà de la perte de poids, offrant une option efficace aux personnes en surpoids et prédiabétiques.
articles.personality_title_es: La dieta keto reduce la grasa del hígado en dos tercios y ayuda a revertir la prediabetes en 4 meses
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas personas con obesidad también tienen exceso de grasa en el hígado y niveles altos de azúcar en la sangre, lo que puede causar problemas graves como la diabetes tipo 2. Los médicos suelen recomendar dietas mediterránea, baja en grasas o baja en carbohidratos para mejorar la salud y perder peso. Pero no estaba claro cuál dieta ayuda más al hígado y al control del azúcar.

**Qué pasó** – Un ensayo clínico comparó tres dietas—cetogénica (muy baja en carbohidratos y alta en grasas), mediterránea y baja en grasas—en 42 adultos con obesidad, prediabetes y enfermedad del hígado graso. Cada persona perdió alrededor del 10 % de su peso en 4 a 5 meses. Los investigadores proporcionaron todas las comidas y revisaron la salud de los participantes regularmente. El grupo keto consumió solo el 4 % de calorías de carbohidratos y 73 % de grasas, mientras que los otros grupos comieron más carbohidratos y menos grasas.

**Impacto** – La dieta keto redujo la grasa del hígado en un 67 %, mucho más que el 45 % de reducción en los otros grupos. Cerca de la mitad del grupo keto ya no tenía prediabetes al terminar el estudio, comparado con menos personas en los otros grupos. Esto muestra que comer menos carbohidratos y más grasas mejora la salud del hígado y el control del azúcar en la sangre de formas que la pérdida de peso sola no explica. Sorprendentemente, el grupo keto no tuvo aumento de grasas o colesterol en la sangre a pesar de consumir más grasas.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores planean hacer estudios más grandes y largos para ver si estos beneficios continúan y cómo se comparan las dietas a largo plazo. También quieren combinar cambios en la dieta con nuevos medicamentos que ayudan a perder peso y controlar el azúcar para tratar mejor la obesidad y sus problemas.

**En una frase** – La dieta cetogénica reduce mucho la grasa del hígado y mejora el control del azúcar en la sangre más allá de la pérdida de peso, ofreciendo una opción efectiva para personas con obesidad y prediabetes.

articles.title: This simple habit is linked to a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's
articles.summary: Reading for pleasure may have surprisingly powerful benefits for the brain, with studies linking it to better memory, reduced stress, improved mental health, and a lower risk of dementia. Researchers highlight findings that just five minutes of fiction can reduce stress by up to 20%, while reading has also been associated with a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.
articles.content:
Reading for enjoyment may offer far more than entertainment. Whether someone prefers a classic Jane Austen novel or a Heartstopper graphic novel, research suggests that reading for pleasure is associated with better mental health, stronger empathy, and a lower risk of dementia.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge are working with The Queen's Reading Room, a charity established by Her Majesty The Queen, to raise awareness of these benefits across all age groups. Their collaboration is part of the National Year of Reading, an initiative encouraging more people to make reading part of their lives.

Cambridge psychiatry researchers Professor Barbara Sahakian and Dr. Christelle Langley began exploring the subject while writing their 2025 book, Brain Boost: Healthy Habits for a Happier Life. They discovered that reading for enjoyment was connected to a remarkably wide range of positive outcomes, yet the amount of research specifically examining these benefits was surprisingly limited.

In a review published in Psychological Medicine, Sahakian and Langley joined Vicki Perrin, CEO of The Queen's Reading Room, to examine the available evidence. Their findings suggest that the format and type of reading matter less than the enjoyment people get from it. They also highlight how reading together, whether through book clubs or parents sharing stories with children, can provide additional benefits.

Professor Sahakian said: "Reading is a great way to support our brain health, develop important cognitive skills and boost our well-being. It's something we ought to be encouraging from an early age, given the increasing evidence of its benefits, particularly to children, but really, it's never too late to start, and it can bring benefits throughout our lives and into old age."

Reading Early in Life Is Linked to Better Brain Development

Despite the growing evidence of its advantages, reading for enjoyment has become less common among young people. Surveys indicate that reading rates among children and teenagers have fallen to their lowest recorded levels, with particularly steep challenges among teenage boys and children from disadvantaged backgrounds.

Even children who are least enthusiastic about reading recognize that it can help them academically. Nearly half acknowledge that books and other reading materials can introduce them to unfamiliar words or teach them something new.

One of the most compelling studies examined more than 10,000 young people. Conducted by Sahakian, Langley, and their colleagues, the research found that children who started reading for pleasure at an early age tended to perform better in several important areas. These included attention, memory, and executive functioning, the mental abilities involved in planning, decision-making, and managing behavior.

Early readers also showed stronger academic performance, experienced fewer mental health problems, and were more likely to develop healthier daily routines. In particular, they tended to get more sleep and spend less time using screens.

Dr. Langley said: "Given how beneficial reading for pleasure is at a young age, we should be doing everything we can to introduce children and young people to reading. The important thing is to find something they'd really enjoy reading about - it might be a TV program or a game - and use this as a way in. Reading comics and graphic novels could also be a helpful introduction as they might be seen as less intimidating, maybe less boring, than novels."

The academic advantages may extend beyond language and literacy. Studies have also connected reading with stronger mathematical performance. Researchers suggest this relationship may arise because both activities rely on some of the same mental abilities, including language processing, memory, and executive function.

Just Five Minutes of Reading May Reduce Stress

The benefits of reading do not disappear after childhood. Among adults, surveys have associated reading for enjoyment with improved emotional well-being, greater relaxation, and reduced stress. Readers also tend to report more empathy, a deeper understanding of other people, and greater openness to viewpoints different from their own.

For many people, books are an especially appealing way to unwind. Reading ranks as the most popular approach to stress relief, with nearly two in five adults (38%) identifying it as their preferred way to relax.

A neuroscience study commissioned by The Queen's Reading Room in 2024 found that spending just five minutes reading fiction could lower stress by as much as 20%. The study also reported improvements in concentration and problem-solving abilities, along with a reduced sense of loneliness.

Books may even provide more comfort than some traditional relaxation habits. In one survey, more respondents said they turned to reading (35%) for comfort than to drinking wine (31%) or taking a hot bath (10%).

Reading Linked to Lower Dementia and Alzheimer's Risk

As people get older, the potential advantages of reading may become especially meaningful. Research has associated mentally stimulating leisure activities, including reading, with slower cognitive decline and a reduced likelihood of developing dementia.

One study followed nearly 5,500 adults aged 55 and older for five years. Participants who regularly took part in activities such as reading were significantly less likely to develop cognitive impairment during the study period.

Another investigation reported an even more striking association. People who read newspapers, magazines, and books had a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.

These findings suggest that keeping the mind engaged through reading may support cognitive health in later life. However, the researchers emphasize that most of the available studies identify associations rather than proving that reading itself prevents dementia.

How Reading May Change the Structure of the Brain

What could explain the many benefits associated with reading? Brain imaging research offers some intriguing clues.

Studies have identified differences in brain structure associated with reading, particularly in regions responsible for language, learning, emotional regulation, and executive control. These differences include greater brain volume and larger cortical areas in certain regions, as well as thicker cortex in areas important for language processing.

Researchers have also observed stronger connections within the brain's white matter, which helps different regions communicate and supports the processing of language.

Although much of this evidence is correlational, some research suggests that reading-related training can directly influence the brain's physical structure.

In one small study involving 11 children with dyslexia between the ages of 7 and 11, researchers tested an eight-week training program designed to strengthen reading abilities. The exercises involved mental imagery, articulation, and tracing letters, combinations of letters, and words.

Following the program, the children demonstrated significant improvements in reading skills. Brain scans also revealed increases in gray matter volume in important regions, providing evidence that reading interventions can be accompanied by measurable structural changes in the brain.

Why Reading Together May Offer Even Greater Benefits

Reading does not have to be a solitary activity. Researchers suggest that sharing books with other people can add a valuable social dimension, creating opportunities for connection and potentially improving both mental and physical well-being.

The Queen's Reading Room has made this idea a central part of its mission. Launched on social media in January 2021, the initiative originally provided a way for people to exchange book recommendations and stay connected during pandemic lockdowns.

It has since expanded into an international community reaching more than 12 million people across 184 countries. Through its flagship festival, neuroscience research, and other programs, the charity works to make reading a more prominent part of everyday life.

Its activities also extend to homeless shelters and domestic violence refuges, where shared reading is used as a therapeutic resource to help people during recovery.

The social connections created through reading groups may be particularly valuable for older adults, who can face increased isolation and reduced opportunities to participate in physically demanding activities.

Professor Sahakian said: "Shared reading groups and book clubs appear to provide additional benefits through social interaction. They can help people feel less isolated and more connected to others, which has been shown to reduce the risk of dementia.

"While these clubs can be fun and beneficial at any age, they're perfect for older people who may not be so mobile - they might not be able to go out as an exercise group or a cycling group, but a reading group is something most people can enjoy."

The researchers' overall message is that people can benefit from reading at any stage of life. Whether someone enjoys novels, newspapers, comics, or stories shared with friends, making time for reading may help support cognitive health, emotional well-being, and social connection.

Vicki Perrin, CEO of The Queen's Reading Room, added: "At The Queen's Reading Room, we have seen first-hand the transformative power of individual and shared reading to change lives. Books truly do make life better, and we're excited to do our bit to help everyone, everywhere, make more room for reading."
articles.reasoning: The article reports on substantial scientific research linking reading for pleasure to significant mental health benefits, including a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease, reduced stress, and improved cognitive function across all ages. It highlights broad societal benefits, including for children, adults, and older adults, with detailed evidence and initiatives promoting reading as a public health intervention.
articles.personality_title: Reading for pleasure linked to lower Alzheimer's risk and better brain health
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Reading is often seen as a pastime, but new research shows it has important benefits for the brain and mental health. Experts from the University of Cambridge and The Queen's Reading Room charity studied how reading for enjoyment affects people of all ages.

**What happened** – Researchers found that reading just five minutes a day can reduce stress by up to 20%. More importantly, adults who read regularly have a 33% lower chance of developing Alzheimer's disease. Studies also show children who start reading for fun early tend to have better memory, attention, and school performance. Reading together, like in book clubs or with parents and children, adds social benefits.

**Impact** – These findings are important because they show reading supports brain health throughout life, not just in childhood. It helps reduce stress, improve mental skills, and may delay dementia. The research suggests that enjoying any kind of reading—novels, comics, newspapers—can be helpful. Reading groups especially help older adults stay connected and reduce loneliness.

**What's next step** – The Queen's Reading Room and Cambridge researchers are promoting reading for all ages through events and programs. They encourage finding books or stories that people enjoy to make reading a regular habit. More studies are planned to understand how reading changes the brain and how reading groups can support mental health.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Reading for pleasure, even for a few minutes daily, supports brain health, lowers stress, and may reduce the risk of Alzheimer's disease.
articles.personality_title_fr: Lire pour le plaisir réduit le risque d'Alzheimer et améliore la santé du cerveau
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La lecture est souvent considérée comme un passe-temps, mais de nouvelles recherches montrent qu'elle a des avantages importants pour le cerveau et la santé mentale. Des experts de l'Université de Cambridge et de l'association The Queen's Reading Room ont étudié comment la lecture pour le plaisir affecte les personnes de tous âges.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Les chercheurs ont découvert que lire seulement cinq minutes par jour peut réduire le stress jusqu'à 20 %. Plus important encore, les adultes qui lisent régulièrement ont 33 % moins de risques de développer la maladie d'Alzheimer. Des études montrent également que les enfants qui commencent à lire pour s'amuser tôt ont une meilleure mémoire, attention et réussite scolaire. Lire ensemble, comme dans des clubs de lecture ou entre parents et enfants, apporte des bienfaits sociaux.

**Impact** – Ces résultats sont importants car ils montrent que la lecture soutient la santé du cerveau tout au long de la vie, pas seulement pendant l'enfance. Elle aide à réduire le stress, améliorer les capacités mentales et peut retarder la démence. La recherche suggère que tout type de lecture appréciée — romans, bandes dessinées, journaux — peut être utile. Les groupes de lecture aident particulièrement les personnes âgées à rester connectées et à réduire la solitude.

**Prochaines étapes** – The Queen's Reading Room et les chercheurs de Cambridge encouragent la lecture à tous les âges grâce à des événements et programmes. Ils recommandent de trouver des livres ou histoires que les gens aiment pour faire de la lecture une habitude régulière. D’autres études sont prévues pour mieux comprendre comment la lecture modifie le cerveau et comment les groupes de lecture peuvent soutenir la santé mentale.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Lire pour le plaisir, même quelques minutes par jour, soutient la santé du cerveau, réduit le stress et peut diminuer le risque d’Alzheimer.

articles.title: Powerful new weight-loss drug helps patients cut knee pain in half
articles.summary: A powerful experimental weight-loss drug helped people with knee osteoarthritis lose about 25% of their body weight at the highest dose, while roughly two-thirds experienced at least a 50% reduction in knee pain. The findings suggest retatrutide could transform treatment for millions suffering from painful arthritis, although its ability to prevent further joint damage remains unknown.
articles.content:
For people living with painful knee osteoarthritis (OA), even simple activities like walking, climbing stairs, or getting out of a chair can become a struggle. Excess body weight can make these challenges even worse. Now, two major clinical trials suggest that a powerful experimental weight-loss drug could provide substantial relief.

The two phase 3 trials, led by Northwestern University, included more than 1,000 participants in total. People receiving the highest dose of retatrutide, an experimental injectable weight-loss medication, lost an average of about 25% of their body weight. When researchers combined the findings from both trials, they found that approximately two-thirds of participants treated with retatrutide reported a reduction in knee pain of at least 50%. By comparison, only 38% of those given a placebo experienced that level of relief.

The benefits extended beyond weight loss and improved knee pain. Participants also showed reductions in blood pressure, blood lipid levels, and inflammation throughout the body.

Findings from both studies were published on Nov. 8 in the New England Journal of Medicine.

"The findings are really saying for people who are overweight and have OA, if you lose a significant amount of weight with this treatment, there is a good chance that you're going to get a meaningful reduction in your knee pain," said corresponding author Dr. Thomas Schnitzer, professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation, anesthesiology and medicine (rheumatology) at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.

"A major factor is that you're loading your knees less and therefore, there's less pain and it allows you to increase your function."

Philip Conaghan, a study co-author and professor of musculoskeletal medicine at the University of Leeds in the United Kingdom, presented results from one of the trials, TRIUMPH-4, on Nov. 8 at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting in Orlando, Florida. Findings from the second trial, TRIUMPH-1-OA, were scheduled for presentation during a separate poster session that same day.

A Potential New Treatment for Millions With Knee Osteoarthritis

Painful knee osteoarthritis affects approximately 5% of Americans (15 million people). Available treatments range from physical therapy and medications applied to the skin to oral anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and Voltaren. Other options include opioids and corticosteroid injections, although the relief provided by steroid injections generally lasts only a short time.

Weight loss is another established way to ease symptoms. Previous studies have shown that losing 5% to 10% of body weight through changes in diet and exercise can improve knee osteoarthritis pain. However, Schnitzer explained that losing more than 10% through these approaches alone is often challenging. For people already struggling with painful knees, exercising enough to achieve substantial weight loss can be especially difficult.

Retatrutide could offer another approach. Developed by Eli Lilly, the experimental medication is administered as a once-weekly injection and works differently from existing GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide and tirzepatide.

While those drugs act on one or two hormone receptors and typically produce weight reductions of 10% to 20%, retatrutide activates receptors associated with three different naturally occurring hormones. In the clinical trials, participants lost approximately 20% to 25% of their body weight, depending on the dose. Eli Lilly scientists also contributed to the research as study co-authors.

"Participants had remarkable responses," Schnitzer said. "Many of the people in this study lost considerable amounts of weight, with a few losing up to a hundred pounds or more."

Why Diet and Exercise Still Matter

Despite the encouraging findings, Schnitzer emphasized that lifestyle changes should remain the starting point for people who are overweight and have painful knee osteoarthritis.

Improving eating habits, increasing physical activity, and making other sustainable lifestyle adjustments can help reduce symptoms without the expense of newer weight-loss medications. These strategies also avoid side effects associated with GLP-1 drugs, including gastrointestinal problems and muscle loss.

Maintaining muscle strength is particularly important for people with knee osteoarthritis because the muscles surrounding the joint help support and stabilize it. Losing too much muscle could therefore create additional challenges for patients who already have difficulty moving comfortably.

For individuals who cannot achieve sufficient weight loss through lifestyle changes and continue to experience significant knee pain, Schnitzer believes retatrutide could become a valuable option if it receives approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Could the Drug Also Slow Knee Arthritis Progression?

Although the trials demonstrated substantial improvements in weight and pain, several important questions remain unanswered.

One of the biggest is whether retatrutide does more than relieve symptoms. Researchers still do not know if the drug can slow the underlying progression of knee osteoarthritis enough to reduce the likelihood that patients will eventually need knee replacement surgery. People who already required a knee replacement were excluded from the trials.

"That would be the goal here to say you can reduce people's pain, and you can stop the progression of their osteoarthritis," Schnitzer said.

Another unanswered question is whether retatrutide might benefit people with painful knee osteoarthritis who are not overweight. Because the trials did not include these patients, further studies will be needed to determine whether they could experience similar improvements.

Researchers are also interested in understanding how much of the pain relief comes directly from weight loss and how much might be related to the drug's effects on inflammation.

"These drugs are believed to have significant anti-inflammatory activity, but the mechanism is not entirely known," Schnitzer said. "Whether cutting down inflammation in the joint is also important in addition to reducing load needs more research, so this is still a first step, in my view. I've been working in the OA field for a long time, and I think this opens up opportunities to do a lot more studies to understand the condition better."

How Researchers Measured Knee Pain Relief

To evaluate changes in symptoms, the research teams used the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC) Pain index, a standardized tool for assessing osteoarthritis pain.

During study visits, participants rated their pain on a scale from 0 to 10. They also used a mobile app to record their pain levels each day, allowing researchers to track how symptoms changed throughout treatment.

The study is titled, "Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity."

articles.personality_title: New weight-loss drug cuts knee pain in half for arthritis patients
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Knee osteoarthritis is a painful condition affecting about 15 million Americans. Extra body weight makes knee pain worse and makes everyday activities harder. Current treatments help some, but many patients still suffer significant pain.

**What happened** – Two large clinical trials tested retatrutide, an experimental weight-loss drug, on over 1,000 people with knee osteoarthritis. Those who took the highest doses lost about 25% of their body weight. Around two-thirds of these patients reported their knee pain dropped by at least half, compared to only 38% in a placebo group. The drug also helped reduce blood pressure, inflammation, and harmful blood fats.

**Impact** – Retatrutide’s strong weight loss helped reduce knee pain significantly, which may improve daily movement and quality of life for many. Unlike current treatments, it works by activating three hormone receptors, leading to more weight loss than similar drugs. This could offer a new option for patients who struggle to lose weight through diet and exercise alone.

**What's next step** – Researchers want to know if retatrutide can also slow down joint damage and reduce the need for knee replacement surgery. They will also study if the drug helps people who are not overweight and how much pain relief comes from weight loss versus reduced inflammation.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Retatrutide shows promise as a powerful new treatment that helps people with knee osteoarthritis lose weight and cut their knee pain in half.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un nouveau médicament contre la perte de poids réduit de moitié la douleur au genou chez les patients arthritiques
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L'arthrose du genou est une maladie douloureuse qui touche environ 15 millions d'Américains. Un excès de poids aggrave la douleur au genou et rend les activités quotidiennes plus difficiles. Les traitements actuels aident certains patients, mais beaucoup souffrent toujours.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Deux grands essais cliniques ont testé le rétatrutide, un médicament expérimental pour la perte de poids, sur plus de 1 000 personnes souffrant d'arthrose du genou. Ceux qui ont pris les doses les plus élevées ont perdu environ 25 % de leur poids corporel. Environ deux tiers ont vu leur douleur au genou diminuer d'au moins 50 %, contre seulement 38 % dans le groupe placebo. Le médicament a aussi aidé à réduire la pression artérielle, l'inflammation et les graisses sanguines nocives.

**Impact** – La forte perte de poids grâce au rétatrutide a réduit la douleur au genou de façon importante, ce qui peut améliorer le mouvement et la qualité de vie. Contrairement aux traitements actuels, il agit sur trois récepteurs hormonaux, ce qui entraîne une perte de poids plus importante que des médicaments similaires. Cela pourrait offrir une nouvelle option pour ceux qui ont du mal à perdre du poids par le régime et l'exercice.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent savoir si le rétatrutide peut aussi ralentir la détérioration des articulations et réduire le besoin de chirurgie. Ils étudieront aussi s'il aide les personnes non en surpoids et combien de la réduction de la douleur vient de la perte de poids ou de la baisse de l'inflammation.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Le rétatrutide montre un grand potentiel comme nouveau traitement aidant à perdre du poids et à réduire de moitié la douleur au genou chez les personnes atteintes d'arthrose.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo medicamento para bajar de peso reduce a la mitad el dolor de rodilla en pacientes con artritis
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La osteoartritis de rodilla es una enfermedad dolorosa que afecta a unos 15 millones de estadounidenses. El exceso de peso empeora el dolor de rodilla y dificulta las actividades diarias. Los tratamientos actuales ayudan a algunos, pero muchos siguen sufriendo.

**Qué pasó** – Dos grandes ensayos clínicos probaron retatrutida, un medicamento experimental para bajar de peso, en más de 1,000 personas con osteoartritis de rodilla. Quienes tomaron las dosis más altas perdieron alrededor del 25 % de su peso corporal. Alrededor de dos tercios reportaron que su dolor de rodilla disminuyó al menos un 50 %, comparado con solo el 38 % en el grupo placebo. El medicamento también ayudó a reducir la presión arterial, la inflamación y las grasas dañinas en la sangre.

**Impacto** – La fuerte pérdida de peso con retatrutida redujo significativamente el dolor de rodilla, mejorando el movimiento diario y la calidad de vida. A diferencia de otros tratamientos, actúa sobre tres receptores hormonales, lo que produce más pérdida de peso que medicamentos similares. Esto podría ofrecer una nueva opción para quienes tienen dificultades para perder peso solo con dieta y ejercicio.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren saber si retatrutida también puede frenar el daño en las articulaciones y reducir la necesidad de cirugía de reemplazo de rodilla. También estudiarán si ayuda a personas sin sobrepeso y cuánto del alivio del dolor proviene de la pérdida de peso o de la reducción de inflamación.

**Resumen en una frase** – Retatrutida promete ser un tratamiento poderoso que ayuda a personas con osteoartritis de rodilla a perder peso y reducir su dolor a la mitad.

articles.content:
Episode Description:

A wristband developed at the University of Nottingham sends small electrical pulses to a nerve in your wrist, and for some people with Tourette’s, their tics settle within moments of switching it on. One 15-year-old called the first time she tried it the best day of her life.

Arielle and Karissa also get into a Greek ship that turned seven years of beach trash into a pollution map, a cancer therapy helping people with Céline Dion’s rare condition walk again, and the real reason you want to cancel plans you were excited to make.

Learn more about April Surac and NeuraSensa: https://www.instagram.com/neurasensa/

If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com.

Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary.

Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram, X, and Blue Sky.

The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy.

Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d

Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes

Transcript:

Welcome and catch-up

Arielle:

Hi, I’m Arielle.

Karissa:

And I’m Karissa.

Arielle:

And welcome to The Optimist Daily’s Weekly Roundup. How are you doing, Karissa?

Karissa:

I’m doing well over here. I’m feeling grateful and grounded as we head into the Thanksgiving week next week here in the US.

Arielle:

Do you have any fun Thanksgiving plans?

Karissa:

Um, I have multiple Thanksgivings actually I’ll be attending.

So this weekend will be my Thanksgiving with my immediate family because everyone is kind of doing different things on actual Thanksgiving Day. And then I’ll be spending actual Thanksgiving with my partner’s family, so multiple celebrations going on this week.

Arielle:

Aw, that’s cute. And speaking of Thanksgiving, we are actually going to be missing next week’s full episode.

We will have just a short greeting from our Optimist Daily family to yours. You can keep an eye out for that, or an ear out for that earlier in the week.

Karissa:

Yeah, exactly. Well, before we head into anything else, Arielle, how is everything with you?

Arielle:

Things are good. I was telling you before we hit record that my personal trainer was here today, and it was-

excruciating. But yeah, it’s, it’s nice to be working on my strength. I think the benefit of working at The Optimist Daily is that you are exposed to so many solutions just for lifestyle changes that are going to help you live a healthier life and a longer life hopefully. And so yeah, even though the workouts are, uh, brutal sometimes-

there’s always light at the end of the tunnel, and I know that it’s for my long-term health, and that kind of motivates me throughout the whole thing.

Stay connected and support our work

Karissa:

There’s just so many great solutions on The Optimist Daily that we get the benefit of learning from. If you want these solutions to your inbox every day, we have a free daily newsletter, and we also have a weekly edition as well.

The link to sign up for that is in the show notes.

Arielle:

We are also on all social media platforms, @optimistdaily on everything except for X. There we are @OdeToOptimism. There you can get more bite-sized versions of full solutions. As always, we welcome any comments, questions, or feedback. You can engage with us on those social platforms.

You can slide into our DMs, or you can email me and Karissa directly at podcast@optimistdaily.com.

Karissa:

We love to hear from you, and we also love when you share all these solutions in any format, whether you’re forwarding the newsletter, sharing this podcast, and leaving a good review, or reposting to your followers.

Arielle:

And it’s a wonderful and free way to support our mission. We are so, so grateful for The Optimist Daily community. You guys make this work so special and so meaningful. We appreciate every single like, follow, share, but we also have huge love for our Emissaries, people who financially donate to The Optimist Daily, whether that’s a one-time thing or a regular monthly or annual donation.

Emissaries help us continue our mission, pushing it forward. Without them, we wouldn’t be able to do this amazing work. If you wanted to become an Emissary, now is a great time to do that, because we set a goal to get 100 new Emissaries by the end of this year. And I think we’ve maybe surpassed the halfway point at this moment in time?

Karissa:

We’re just about halfway there, yeah, to our Emissary goal. So help us cross that finish line by the end of the year so we can start off 2027 on an optimistic note, and just get these solutions to as many people as possible.

This week’s solutions

Arielle:

Well, with all of that said, shall I jump into the solutions of the week?

Karissa:

Yeah, let’s get into all the positive news.

“8 simple habits time management experts say build a better morning”

Arielle:

The first solution we have is a lifestyle solution, something that all of us can apply to our lives right now to make it better, and the title is “8 simple habits time management experts say build a better morning.”

So this is especially for those of us who have a lot of flexibility regarding our schedule, for our remote workers and the like. But do you know when it’s 2:00 PM and you, you can’t really say where the morning went? Two time management experts say the fix for this doesn’t start when your alarm goes off.

It actually starts the night before, and it’s way less intense than the really popular two-hour routines that are all over social media that, like, incorporate a bunch of, I don’t know, early morning journaling, and a stretching routine, and an ice plunge, and whatever the latest wellness trends are. Yeah.

It can be a lot more simple. I think a lot of us will not be surprised that the number one morning habit, according to Julie Morgenstern, is about your phone. No screens for the first hour after you wake up and the last hour before bed. She compares managing phone time to managing sugar, and I have to say, I am not good at this.

Karissa:

Yeah. I, I am not good at managing sugar or screen time, so that’s a good comparison.

Arielle:

Yeah. I, uh… It’s so tempting, especially with the alarm on my phone. I swipe to turn the alarm off, and suddenly I’m already looking at the screen. So I think an analog old-school alarm clock might be a pretty good fix for this.

Another habit that she says starts the morning off on the right foot is to begin the workday with the hardest, most important task. So even if the rest of the day falls apart, you’ve done the thing that matters most, that has the most impact. These are all really kind of simple things that you can do or keep in mind when you’re going through your morning.

Karissa, what’s the first thing you do when you wake up?

Karissa:

Well, I mean, I do look at my phone first thing because I’m also swiping to turn off my alarm. So in turn, I’m also looking at all those notifications for a second before I get out of bed, and then I do have my little morning routine. I’ll get up, wash my face, brush my teeth, feed my cat, and put on a pot of coffee, and get some breakfast going.

What about you?

Arielle:

After I have that quick minute on my phone, I also set the kettle to make my tea, and while that’s boiling, I’ll brush my teeth and usually do a little tidy up of the house because this is also my office, so I can’t focus if it’s kind of messy. Luckily, my dog makes me go out.

So I do have, like, 20 to 30 minutes of just being out in nature and getting as much sunlight as I can, and I think that counts as one of these microbursts of self-care, which is defined as 5 to 20 minutes of doing something that recharges you. According to this article, the ideal morning routine has three or four elements max.

Anything more and you’re setting yourself up for feeling guilty for missing something on a certain morning, or if you have, like, a long checklist of things to do, then it can put a lot of pressure on you as well. Um, so yeah, I did also like that aspect of the article that really emphasizes that it doesn’t have to be complicated.

We’re not going through all of the tips here, like what to do the night before, but I highly recommend you check out the article for some more morning routine inspo.

Karissa:

Yeah, 100%.

“This Tourette’s wrist device cut tics by a quarter in a UK trial”

Arielle:

All right. The next solution is titled “This Tourette’s wrist device cut tics by a quarter in a UK trial.” There’s a wristband out of the University of Nottingham that sends tiny electrical pulses to a nerve in your wrist, and for some people with Tourette’s, it calms their tics the moment they switch it on.

One 15-year-old called the first time she tried it the best day of her life. I actually have a cousin who has Tourette’s. And his tics are not so… They’re, they… Like, he can go through the world and navigate it fine, but you can tell that he’s putting a lot of energy towards suppressing a lot as well.

Yeah. I can only imagine how life-changing a device like this is that’s kind of subtle and elegant and simple and has a really big impact on just the mental and physical space that suppressing tics has, and also just having to go through the world with people staring at you, not really understanding what’s going on.

The source for this article came from the BBC, and I actually took a minute to watch their video on this, and I highly recommend watching the video so that you can kind of get a better sense for how much impact this small device has on people.

Karissa:

Yeah. And how exactly does it work?

Arielle:

So how it works is kind of wild.

There’s rhythmic pulses to the median nerve cha- which changes activity in the parts of the brain that control movement. In a trial of 121 people, tics dropped by about 25% on average, and it even works for people who don’t have Tourette’s. There was another teenager named Ollie, and he has a functional neurological disorder which makes his neck move constantly without him having any control over it.

And when he tried the device, it also just completely stopped the neck movements. There’s a lot of potential for this wearable neurotech to positively affect the lives of people with Parkinson’s tremors or anxiety or even OCD.

“Animal welfare ballot measures had a strong night in the 2026 midterms”

Arielle:

The next solution is titled “Animal welfare ballot measures had a strong night in the 2026 midterms.”

Okay, so we’ve already talked about the midterms, but we haven’t talked about this specific area of it. I think most people have never eaten foie gras in their lives, and yet it produced some of the most lopsided votes of election night. Animals came out of these midterms surprisingly well, and there’s a pattern in what passed and what didn’t that I found quite interesting.

First of all, do you know how foie gras is made? Have you ever eaten it, Karissa?

Karissa:

Never eaten it, and I didn’t really know much about it until this article actually.

Arielle:

Yeah. I, I wanna say I have never tried it, but I can’t be for certain. I, I- worked a lot in the hospitality industry and, uh, tried a lot of different things, but it makes me feel a bit bad if I, if I had, because they basically, like, force feed ducks.

Karissa:

Yeah.

Arielle:

Um, or is it geese? But they- I think it’s geese, yeah … force feed them, and it produces this pâté-like, um I’m not describing this well, but people who know foie gras, you know what I’m talking about. Yeah. And those of you who don’t, look it up ’cause it is a l- well, it’s kinda disturbing. Um, so DC voted 73% and Denver 66% to ban foie gras sales, and a DC chef has been hosting foie gras tasting dinners to fund a lawsuit against the ban.

So, yeah. Oh. There’s a, a little bit of tension there.

Karissa:

Yeah.

Arielle:

Colorado rejected a constitutional right to hunt and fish, and the fight came down to two words: traditional methods, which critics said could have brought back leg-hold traps and poison as, um, as hunting strategies. Denver voters said no to banning fur and slaughterhouses in 2024, but yes to banning foie gras now.

So it seems like narrow bans on one practice seem to have a much easier time going through than ones that take on a whole industry for, of course, concerns about employment and yeah, having to restructure or get rid of a whole industry. Um-

so more people are actually paying attention to how their food is produced, even when they’re not really changing their diet.

Like, they’re not going vegan, they’re not going vegetarian, but they are concerned about how their food is produced and where it comes from.

“The Greek coastline cleanup that turned trash into a pollution map”

Arielle:

The next solution is titled “The Greek coastline cleanup that turned trash into a pollution map.” The team that’s doing the cleanup isn’t just picking up trash.

They’re noting down every single piece of it. This project consists of one ship, 20 people, five inflatable boats, and 1,140 tons of trash pulled off remote shores since 2019. For a visual, that’s 22 Olympic swimming pools’ worth of pollution. They’ve built what they say is the largest marine pollution database in the Mediterranean, and university researchers are using it to map plastic on the seabed.

The data led them somewhere they didn’t necessarily expect. A lot of the trash came from inland, from rivers and illegal dumps, so they also started a second program on land. Beach cleanups are pretty popular, but there’s growing frustration that cleaning up the beach doesn’t necessarily stop the flow, or it doesn’t nip the issue in the bud.

But it’s nice to see that citizen science and cleanup data are increasingly shaping policy on plastics.

“April Surac built NeuraSensa so art adapts to the people using it”

Arielle:

The last solution that I’m going to share with you before I hand it over to Karissa is a Local Changemaker. This one’s titled “April Surac built NeuraSensa so art adapts to the people using it.” This week’s Local Changemaker is April Surac, a Florida teenager who grew up in her family’s furniture workshop and has a younger sister who has autism.

Her installations are made of fabric with sensors built in, so the surfaces shift under your hand and the light and sound change as you move through the room. They’re designed for people with autism and people with sensory or cognitive differences, including dementia. More than 15,000 people have experienced the installations, and she sent over 250 sensory kits to families, schools, and hospitals.

And she funds a lot of it with her own savings. I think she started this when she was only 16 or 17, which is so impressive. She’s also a 2025 Barron Prize winner, and she’s now working on gallery commissions in New York, LA, and London. Plus, she is developing a wearable sensory tool, and she’s moving towards patents for that.

I think it’s really encouraging that a lot of people are growing in their awareness and compassion for diverse bodies and experiences. Sensory-friendly hours are popping up at museums, grocery stores, and movie theaters, which comes from people just realizing how much public spaces assume about our bodies.

It’s wonderful to see the shift from accessibility compliance to designing for everyone from the very beginning of a project.

Karissa:

Yeah, exactly. And I really loved that she had a line that said, “Design should adapt to people, not the other way around.” And that’s something we don’t see enough of in our world.

So I think this is just such a fascinating, uh, story, what she’s doing, and I feel so honored to be able to share her story here on The Optimist Daily as one of our local changemakers this year.

“US homelessness decline hits its steepest one-year drop in a decade”

Karissa:

“US homelessness decline hits its steepest one-year drop in a decade.” So homelessness in the US dropped more than 6% last year.

That’s about 49,000 fewer people without housing, and the biggest one-year drop in over a decade. One of the biggest points here in this article is that veteran homelessness is down nearly 60% since 2010, and advocates say it’s proof that putting people in housing first with no strings attached actually works.

On the other hand, the Trump administration credits immigration enforcement and encampment crackdowns to this decline, but advocates say their data shows cities with camping bans did worse than average. It’s important to note, too, that not everyone saw a drop because people who’ve been homeless for a long time increased slightly, and that’s the group that both sides are fighting over the best way to help them.

But yeah, I mean, in a time where housing affordability is one of the biggest issues in the country right now, this is encouraging news nonetheless.

“Dreading plans you made yourself? There’s a name for that feeling”

Karissa:

The next solution is another lifestyle one, and it’s “Dreading plans you made yourself? There’s a name for that feeling.” So you know when you’re the one who made the plans, and then an hour before you’re supposed to leave, you’re on the couch drafting a text reading, “I’m so sorry, something came up,” or, “I feel sick.”

There’s actually a name for this experience, and there’s a surprisingly simple trick for getting out the door anyway. Arielle, have you had this feeling before?

Arielle:

Oh my gosh, this is so relatable. I do find myself kind of dreading plans, and I try not to cancel. I try to push myself through it, but there are some days where I’m just like, “Ooh, I don’t wanna hop on my bike and go through the rain,” and-

you know, I don’t wanna see anyone. I don’t wanna talk to anyone. I’m so tired. So yeah, this solution definitely spoke to me.

Karissa:

And I’m sure probably all of us have been there at some point or another. But this feeling is called anticipatory anxiety. 55% of Gen Z say they feel relief when plans get canceled, and a UK survey found that 68% of under 34s have flaked.

But there’s a simple therapist-approved trick to get over this anxiety. Set an alarm for when you need to start getting ready, and when it goes off, shower and get dressed without debating it. So kind of just going forward with it without overthinking it. I think flaking has become so normal now that some people kind of dread planning anything, including their own birthdays and events.

And in a time where loneliness is being talked about as a public health issue, canceling plans is a small part of this bigger picture. I feel like it’s kind of a lot easier to cancel plans, too, especially ’cause you don’t even have to call someone to cancel. You just send a text. But usually it’s better for all of us to push through and go forward with that connection anyways.

Arielle:

I like how this article said that part of the strategy is to imagine a moment when you did push through and you did go to whatever event or whatever gathering or, or meetup that you were once dreading. And chances are you ended up enjoying yourself, and you forgot all about that dread that you had before you actually stepped out the door.

And there’s a lot of discussion around protecting our own peace, which I think is valid, but it can make it a lot easier to cop out. We have to be really careful about whether or not we are protecting our peace and we do need that break, because sometimes we definitely do need to take a moment for ourselves, or if we’re just letting the anxiety take over.

“Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers”

Karissa:

Well, moving on to the next solution, “Bans cut two forever chemicals by 30 percent in England’s rivers.” Two of the most toxic forever chemicals have dropped by almost a third in England’s rivers over the last 10 years, and in fish by about half. The UK basically banned PFOS in 2010 and PFOA in 2020, and the river data now shows the effect, that 30% and 29% drops.

But the catch is the chemicals didn’t actually disappear. The total amount is probably the same, but it’s just been diluted and washed out to sea. So it’s still out there, but there’s not as much, you know, going in. There are about 15,000 types of PFAS, and England has just two facilities that can destroy them for good, so not a lot, uh, out there that can get them out of here.

PFAS are in the news constantly. They’re in our drinking water, in non-stick pans, rain jackets, and people are increasingly worried about them in their own homes, with good reason of course, because they don’t go away. And the UK government just announced it will start measuring forever chemicals in people’s bodies, so we should have more data on, you know, how exactly forever these chemicals are, and hopefully that will inform more policy in the future.

“CAR-T therapy helps stiff person syndrome patients walk and work again”

Karissa:

The next solution is “CAR-T therapy helps stiff person syndrome patients walk and work again.” Stiff person syndrome is a rare condition that Céline Dion lives with, and until now, there’s been no real treatment for it. Doctors at the Mayo Clinic tried a therapy that’s normally used for cancer, and some patients who needed help walking are now miraculously back at work.

CAR-T therapy is something that takes your own immune cells, reprograms them in a lab, and puts them back to wipe out the cells causing the disease. Patients in this one got a single treatment, and one patient, Jonathan, went from needing his family’s help with basic tasks to returning to his favorite hobbies like hunting and fishing again, and he says he hasn’t had a single episode since.

This condition, like I mentioned at the beginning, was, you know, kind of brought into the spotlight by Céline Dion’s diagnosis in 2022. She was part of a documentary that brought this condition to the fore. So yeah, CAR-T therapies are one of the biggest stories in medicine right now, and researchers are also trying it out on lupus, MS, and other autoimmune diseases.

But as of now, these therapies are incredibly expensive, so it raises the questions about who will have access to them. But hopefully with all medical breakthroughs and advancements, it will become more accessible to more people who need it.

“6 hosting habits that leave holiday guests feeling uneasy (and how to avoid them)”

Karissa:

The last solution I have to share is also a lifestyle-oriented one, and has to do kind of with Thanksgiving and the holidays coming up.

“6 hosting habits that leave holiday guests feeling uneasy (and how to avoid them).” So yeah, this holiday party season is about to start, and this one’s all about the stuff your guests notice but would never mention. This goes over a lot of great, uh, you know, pointers about hosting. One prominent one is the parking and coats problem.

A party can be beautifully decorated and still feel chaotic if peoples have to circle the block searching for parking, or if they have to hold their jackets for 30 minutes without somewhere to put them.

Arielle:

The tip that spoke to me was about letting yourself as a host enjoy the gathering as well, instead of always being concerned with, like, cleaning up or prepping things or grabbing whatever, because the people who are there, the people you invited, are there to presumably spend time with you and each other. And it can put people on edge if you’re just constantly, like, fluttering around and, you know, making sure that everything is running perfectly without actually taking the time to settle in.

And that, that is kind of challenging for me. Um, especially because I enjoy cleaning. But that’s definitely something that I’m going to be taking to heart this holiday season. And yeah, there’s a lot of other really great tips here as well. But yeah, exciting to get into the festive spirit.

Karissa:

That’s all the solutions we had this week on The Optimist Daily.

Closing quote

Arielle:

Before we wrap up this episode, we have an inspiring quote, as usual.

Karissa:

Yes. The quote is, “My turn shall also come: I sense the spreading of a wing.” And that’s from Osip Mandelstam. Very poetic. Yeah, a poetic end to this edition of the weekly roundup.

Thanksgiving sign-off

Arielle:

Yes. We will be back… Oh, we won’t actually be back next week with a full episode, but we will have a special Thanksgiving greeting from The Optimist Daily team to all of you. But in the meantime, Karissa and I wish you all a very, very happy, restful weekend.

articles.personality_title: New wristband eases Tourette’s tics, offering hope to many
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**
Tourette’s syndrome causes sudden, repeated movements or sounds called tics. Many people with Tourette’s struggle to control these tics, which can affect their daily lives.

**What happened**
Researchers at the University of Nottingham created a wristband that sends tiny electrical pulses to a nerve in the wrist. In a trial with 121 people, this device reduced tics by about 25%. A 15-year-old who used it said it was the best day of her life. The wristband works by sending rhythmic pulses to the median nerve, which helps calm the brain areas that control movement.

**Impact**
This wristband is small, easy to wear, and can help people feel more comfortable and confident. It could change life for many who have Tourette’s or other movement disorders, like Parkinson’s tremors or anxiety. Because it works quickly and without medicine, it offers a new way to manage symptoms.

**What’s next step**
Scientists are exploring how this technology can help other conditions. Wider use and more trials could make the wristband available to more people. Meanwhile, research continues on related health breakthroughs, like CAR-T therapy helping rare diseases, showing progress in medical treatments.

**One-sentence takeaway**
A wristband sending gentle pulses to the wrist can reduce Tourette’s tics, giving new relief to patients and opening doors for future treatments.
